title: Your pipeline succeeded. Why is the dashboard wrong?
learningObjective: Recognise a join fan-out (one-to-many join inflating a SUM), diagnose it with row and distinct-order counts, and repair it by picking one deterministic latest-status row per order before joining.

segments.text: Your pipeline succeeded. Every test is green. So why is the dashboard wrong?
Finance says paid revenue is ₹600. The dashboard says ₹1,800.
segments.speech: Finance says paid revenue is six hundred rupees. The dashboard says eighteen hundred rupees.

segments.text: Nothing crashed. The join changed the grain, meaning what one row represents.
The load job and the row-count test only prove the data arrived. Neither checks what one row means.
Take three paid orders: ₹100, ₹200, and ₹300.
segments.speech: Take three paid orders: one hundred, two hundred, and three hundred rupees.

segments.text: Each order has three status changes in the history table.
Join every history row, and each order is copied three times.
Nine rows now. Sum them, and ₹600 becomes ₹1,800.
segments.speech: Nine rows now. Sum them, and six hundred rupees becomes eighteen hundred.

segments.text: That is a one-to-many join. The amount repeats for every history row.
To catch it, compare counts. Nine joined rows, but only three distinct orders.
Then inspect one order. Order 102 shows the same ₹200 three times.
segments.speech: Then inspect one order. Order one oh two shows the same two hundred rupees three times.

segments.text: Same order, same amount, three rows. Every extra history row adds the amount again.
For a current-status report, pick one latest history row per order before joining.
Sort each order's history by time, break ties with the history ID, and keep the first row.
segments.speech: Sort each order's history by time, break ties with the history I D, and keep the first row.

segments.text: Without that tie-breaker, two rows with the same timestamp could swap places between runs.
Now each order matches exactly one row. Three orders, three rows.
The total is ₹600 again, and the counts agree.
segments.speech: The total is six hundred rupees again, and the counts agree.

segments.text: The fix did not change the data. It changed which rows reach the join.
Need orders that were ever paid? That is different logic: check whether any history row says paid.
And SUM(DISTINCT amount) is not a general fix. Two different orders can share the same amount.
segments.speech: And sum distinct amount is not a general fix. Two different orders can share the same amount.

segments.text: DISTINCT removes repeated values, not duplicate rows. Those are different things.
So when a total looks wrong, check the grain. Count the rows, then count the orders.

params.wrongSql:
SELECT SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_status_history h
  ON h.order_id = o.order_id;
params.fixedSql:
WITH latest AS (
  SELECT order_id, status FROM (
    SELECT order_id, status, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY order_id
      ORDER BY changed_at DESC, id DESC) rn
    FROM order_status_history) t
  WHERE rn = 1)
SELECT SUM(o.amount) AS revenue FROM orders o
JOIN latest l USING (order_id)
WHERE l.status = 'paid';

sources.title: PostgreSQL tutorial: Joins Between Tables
sources.note: Join semantics: each matching pair of rows produces an output row.

reviewNotes.text: The dataset is illustrative, not real data. Every sample order ends in status paid.

The failing query deliberately has no status filter, to isolate join grain. A WHERE h.status = 'paid' on the full history would hide this fan-out in the sample; real bugs usually filter on a different column or not at all. Decide whether to mention this.
ROW_NUMBER() syntax is valid in SQLite/Postgres. Snowflake and BigQuery offer QUALIFY as a shorter form. Tie-break assumes history id increases with insertion order.
Order 104 in the SUM(DISTINCT) card is not in the main dataset; the arithmetic (200 + 200 = 400, DISTINCT gives 200) is shown only on that card.
